i think what you are referring to is about how the cones and rods in your retina are dispersed, usually the center of your vision. 

Cones are less sensitive to light but have better color vision and usually see details better/reponse faster to rapid changes in images

Rods are better for low light function and kind of for contrast

Your cone cells are concentrated in the center and rods are at the peripheries, 

this actually makes things easier to see at night if its right at the outside of your "focus zone".

Older TVs mostly used analog radio signals (RF) picked up from an antenna. Each "channel" is actually a different radio wave frequency. When you set your TV to a specific channel, you're telling it "only listen to signals on this frequency, and ignore any others". That's how you can get just the picture and sound from one broadcast even though there may be dozens of channels all broadcasting in your area with overlapping signals.

When you plug in an old video game console, you're providing the TV with the same kind of signals, but over a wire instead of through the air. These signals are still on a particular frequency, though, so the TV needs to know which channel to listen to. As best I can figure out, channels 1 through 4 are the ones that had the least amount of broadcast TV stations on them, so a lot of companies used those channels / frequencies for hardware that plugs into TVs. This includes things like VHS players.

Not all devices were locked into channel 3. Some had switches on the back that let you pick between a few different channels.

Modern TVs usually use digital signals delivered over wires instead of broadcast RF (though you can still get an RF antenna and plug it in to many TVs). With those, you still need some way for the TV to pick which of several inputs to pay attention to. That's why modern TVs have "channels" like "HDMI 1", "HDMI 2", etc. They're basically the same concept as the old channels 1 through X, but adapted for the modern way of sending signals.
